passages.t: Eliphaz: is not your wickedness great?
passages.happening:
‘Then Eliphaz the Temanite replied’ (verse 1). “Can a man be of use to God? Can even a wise man benefit Him? Does it delight the Almighty that you are righteous? Does He profit if your ways are blameless?” (verses 2-3). God would not punish Job for being devout. “Is not your wickedness great? Are not your iniquities endless?” (verse 5).

Then Eliphaz lists Job's crimes. He took pledges from his brothers for no reason and stripped the naked of their clothes. ‘You gave no water to the weary and withheld food from the famished’ (verse 7). ‘You sent widows away empty-handed, and the strength of the fatherless was crushed’ (verse 9). That, he says, is why snares surround Job, why darkness covers him and a flood overwhelms him.
passages.hearers:
The third and last round begins. Eliphaz, who always speaks first and is usually taken to be the eldest, has moved a long way. In chapters 4 and 5 he spoke gently and assumed Job was basically righteous. In chapter 15 he accused Job of undermining piety with his words. Now, with no evidence at all, he charges Job with specific crimes.

His logic, in the form he would sign: God gains nothing from anyone, so he cannot be punishing Job for his goodness. God punishes sin. Job's suffering is great. So his sin must be great.

His charges assume the duties of a great landowner. He was expected to protect the vulnerable: to lend to the needy, provide for widows and orphans and judge fairly. A pledge was property held as security for a loan, and for the poor it was often a cloak that served as a blanket at night. Refusing water and bread broke the old duty of hospitality, and widows and orphans had no man to speak for them in court.

Eliphaz has a point in verses 2 and 3. God does not need anything from his creatures. But he draws the wrong conclusion, that God does not care about the righteous. The prologue showed the opposite: God delights in Job (1:8).
passages.later: Israel's law protected the poor man's cloak: ‘If you take your neighbor’s cloak as collateral, return it to him by sunset, because his cloak is the only covering he has for his body’ (Exodus 22:26-27).
passages.hard:
Why does Eliphaz accuse Job of crimes he never committed?

Nothing in the book supports the charges. The narrator and God both call Job blameless and upright (1:1; 1:8; 2:3), and Job's own account of his life in chapters 29 and 31 shows him as a defender of widows, orphans and the poor.

The most common explanation is that Eliphaz reasons backward from his theology. If God always punishes in proportion to sin, then great suffering proves great sin, and Eliphaz simply supplies the sins his system requires. Some interpreters add that he picks the likeliest crimes for a rich man, the abuses the powerful were known for. Others note that he may sincerely believe he is being kind, since naming the sin is the first step toward the restoration he promises at the end of the speech.

On every reading the chapter is a sober warning about what happens when a theology is trusted more than a person's own testimony and God's own verdict. No one may invent sins for a suffering person because their suffering seems to require them.
passages.asks: Eliphaz supplied the sins his theory needed. Ask whether you have ever assumed the worst about someone because of what happened to them. And ask whose account of their own life you have refused to believe.

passages.happening:
“Is not God as high as the heavens? Look at the highest stars, how lofty they are!” (verse 12). Eliphaz puts words in Job's mouth: what does God know? Can he judge through thick darkness, with clouds veiling him as he walks the vault of heaven?

“Will you stay on the ancient path that wicked men have trod? They were snatched away before their time, and their foundations were swept away by a flood” (verses 15-16). They told God to leave them alone, though it was God who filled their houses with good things. The righteous see their end and are glad.
passages.hearers:
Ancient people often pictured the sky as a vault or circle over the earth, with God enthroned above it and hidden by clouds. Eliphaz accuses Job of thinking that the clouds keep God from seeing. Job has never said this. His complaint has been that God sees him far too closely (7:17-20).

Many interpreters hear in the wicked men whose foundations were swept away an allusion to the generation of Noah's flood.

Verse 18 repeats almost word for word a line Job had just spoken (21:16), as if Eliphaz were throwing Job's own words back at him.
passages.asks: Eliphaz answered things Job had never said. Ask whether you have ever argued against a version of someone that was not really them. And ask what it would take to answer the person instead.

passages.happening:
“Reconcile now and be at peace with Him; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from His mouth, and lay up His words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty, you will be restored” (verses 21-23).

If Job will throw his gold into the dust, ‘then the Almighty will be your gold and the finest silver for you’ (verse 25). Then he will delight in God and lift up his face. He will pray, and God will hear. Light will shine on his ways. And he will even be able to pray for others: ‘He will deliver even one who is not innocent, rescuing him through the cleanness of your hands’ (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
This is the most beautiful poetry in any of the friends' speeches. Return, shuv, is the Old Testament's central word for repentance, and the prophets use it again and again. The promise that God himself will be Job's gold, when he lets his gold go, is a true insight: God is the treasure that replaces all others. Ophir was famous for the finest gold; where it lay is unknown.

The contrast between the harsh middle of the speech and its tender end shows a man who sincerely believes that accusing Job is the first step in helping him. His counsel is good in itself. He is urging repentance for sins Job did not commit.

The last verse holds an irony the reader will only see at the end. The Hebrew of its first line is uncertain, and some translations read it as delivering the innocent. Either way, Eliphaz promises that the returning sinner will be able to rescue others by his prayers. In 42:8 it is Job, the man Eliphaz wrongly accused, who prays for Eliphaz.
passages.later: The psalm of the law uses Eliphaz's picture of laying up God's words: “I have hidden Your word in my heart that I might not sin against You” (Psalm 119:11).
passages.asks: Eliphaz said that God himself would be Job's treasure. Ask whether that is true for you, or whether something else is your gold. And ask whether your call to someone else to return to God is ever really a way of saying you are right.
